abstract: We characterise optimal tax policies when the government has access to consumption taxation and cannot credibly commit to future policies. We consider a neoclassical economy where factor income taxation is distortionary within the period, due to endogenous labour and capital utilisation and non-tax-deductibility of depreciation. Contrary to the case where only labour and capital income are taxed, the optimal time-consistent policies with consumption taxation are remarkably similar to their Ramsey counterparts. The welfare gains from commitment are negligible, while they are substantial without consumption taxation. Further, the welfare gains from taxing consumption are much higher without commitment.
summary_en: Standard optimal-taxation analysis assumes governments can credibly commit to future tax policies. Laczó and Rossi study what happens when commitment is impossible — a more realistic case in many democracies. Crucially, when consumption taxation is available alongside labour and capital income taxes, the time-consistent optimal policy looks remarkably similar to the Ramsey full-commitment benchmark. Welfare gains from commitment are negligible. Without consumption taxation, the gains from commitment are substantial. The result strengthens the case for consumption taxation as a robustness device in fiscal frameworks where political-cycle commitment is fragile.
data_used: Theoretical model — neoclassical economy with endogenous labour and capital utilisation, calibrated to standard US data. No primary dataset.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian fiscal-policy design at the Pénzügyminisztérium. Hungary relies heavily on consumption taxation (VAT at 27%, the EU's highest) — the paper provides theoretical justification: in environments where governments cannot credibly commit to future policy (e.g., due to election cycles), consumption taxation is a robust optimal-policy substitute. Useful framework for ÁKK debt-strategy assumptions.
title: Time-consistent consumption taxation
